A speech to the next generation retains the cost of earlier choices

Moses is speaking to the children of the people who refused at Kadesh. He says “you” throughout, as if they had been there (verses 26–27). The parents’ choice is told as the family’s own history. In verse 37 he adds his own loss: he also will not enter. He says it was “for your sakes,” tying his fate to theirs. Numbers 20:12 gives the reason as Moses’s own act at the rock. So the speech keeps the cost of the past in front of a new generation.
The land promise does not give Israel every neighboring territory

Israel is on its way to land God promised. Verse 5 says the promise has edges. Mount Seir belongs to Esau, “because I have given” it to him. Verses 9 and 19 say the same of Moab and Ammon, Lot’s children. So the LORD gives land to other peoples too, and Israel must respect it. Israel is to buy food and water there, not take it (verse 6). Sihon’s land is given to Israel, and he refuses peace (verses 24–30).
Moses must prepare a successor for work he cannot finish

Moses’s prayer in verses 24–25 is personal: let me see the good land. The answer is a flat no: “Speak no more to me of this matter.” He may look from a mountain but not cross (verse 27). Verse 28 turns at once to what he can still do. He is to appoint Joshua, encourage him, and strengthen him. Joshua will finish the work, and Moses must make him ready for it. Verses 21–22 show Moses already doing this.
A remembered voice limits what an image can claim

Verse 12 states what happened at Horeb: a voice, and no form. Verse 15 draws the rule from that fact. Because they saw no shape, they may make no shape to stand for God. Verses 16–18 close every door: human, animal, bird, creeping thing, fish. What Israel was given is words, written on two tablets (verse 13). So God is remembered by his words, taught to children (verse 9). An image would claim to show what no one saw.
The command to rest receives an explanation rooted in slavery

Exodus 20:11 tied the Sabbath to God’s rest at creation. Verse 15 gives a second reason: “you were a servant in the land of Egypt.” Verse 14 says servants must rest “as well as you.” A master must remember being a slave when he sees his workers. Pharaoh gave Israel no rest (Exodus 5:5–9). So the weekly rest is a way of not becoming Pharaoh. Verse 3 adds that the covenant is with the living hearers, not only their parents.
Memory needs daily practice

Verse 5 asks for love with the whole person. Verse 6 says where the words must be: on the heart. Verse 7 turns that inward state into a daily habit with children. The four settings cover a whole day: sitting, walking, lying down, rising. No special place or teacher is named. Verses 10–12 show why the habit is needed: full houses make people forget. Verse 20 expects it to work, since the child starts asking questions.
Chosen status does not rest on numerical strength

Verses 1–5 give Israel hard orders against seven nations. Verse 6 calls Israel chosen, and verse 7 blocks a proud reading of that word. They were not more in number; they were the fewest. Verse 8 gives two reasons, and both lie in God: his love and his oath. So being chosen is not a reward for strength or goodness. Verse 4 gives the stated reason for the harsh orders: the pull of other gods. The chapter states those orders plainly and does not soften them.
Success can hide the conditions that made it possible

The danger in this chapter is plenty, not hunger. Verses 12–13 list good houses, growing herds, silver, and gold. Verse 14 says a full heart is “lifted up” and forgets. Verse 17 gives the thought that follows: my own hand got me this wealth. In the wilderness no one could think that, since manna fell each day. Verse 18 corrects it: God gives the power to get wealth. He gives it to keep the covenant he swore, not to prove their worth.
Possessing the land does not prove the people's innocence

Winning a land could make a people think they deserved it. Verses 4, 5, and 6 each deny that. The nations lose the land for their wickedness. Israel gains it because of God’s oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Verse 6 adds a hard name for Israel: “a stiff-necked people.” Verses 7–24 back it up with the calf and four other failures. So possession of the land proves God’s faithfulness, not Israel’s merit.
Remembered exclusion becomes a duty toward resident outsiders

Verse 17 describes God at his greatest: God of gods, mighty, taking no bribes. Verse 18 says what that great God does. He gives justice to the fatherless and widow and feeds and clothes the foreigner. Verse 19 draws the command from his example: “Therefore love the foreigner.” It adds Israel’s own memory: “you were foreigners in the land of Egypt.” So the duty has two roots, who God is and what Israel went through. Verse 16 calls this a change of heart, not only of rules.
A description of farming turns the land into a place of dependence

Verse 10 recalls Egyptian farming: water moved to the seed “with your foot.” The farmer there brought the water himself. Verse 11 says Canaan “drinks water from the rain of the sky.” No one can make it rain. So the new land ties each harvest to the one who sends rain (verse 14). Verses 16–17 state the risk: other gods, a shut sky, no fruit. The land itself becomes a daily lesson in dependence.
A central place of worship does not control every meal

Verses 5–14 gather all offerings into one place that God will choose. That could seem to make every meal of meat a long journey. Verse 15 prevents this. People may kill and eat “within all your gates,” like game. The unclean and the clean may both eat it, so it is ordinary food. Only the blood rule follows them home (verse 16). The text never names the chosen place.
A striking sign does not settle whether a message should be followed

Verse 2 grants that the sign “comes to pass.” The test is not whether the wonder is real. The test is where the message leads: “Let’s go after other gods.” A true sign joined to that call must be refused (verse 3). So a message is judged by loyalty to the LORD who freed them (verse 5). Verse 14 adds a rule for rumor: inquire, investigate, and ask diligently. The penalties are severe, and the town’s case requires proof first.
A tithe can serve people who lack a secure household share

In most years the family eats its tithe at the chosen place (verses 22–26). Verse 28 changes the plan every third year. The whole tithe is stored “within your gates,” in the home town. Verse 29 names four groups: the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow. The Levite has no land, and the others have no secure provider. They are to “eat and be satisfied,” not just get by. The blessing on the farmer’s work is tied to this sharing.
An approaching release must not become an excuse to refuse help

Verse 1 cancels debts every seventh year. That creates a temptation, and verse 9 names it. A lender could refuse a loan that will soon be wiped out. The verse calls that thought wicked, and the poor may cry to the LORD. Verse 10 asks for more than the loan: a heart that does not grudge it. Verses 13–14 say a freed servant must not leave empty-handed. Verse 15 gives the reason: Israel was a slave, and the LORD redeemed it.
Festival joy reaches beyond the people who own its resources

The feast of weeks comes at harvest, when a landowner has the most. Verse 11 says who must rejoice with him. The list starts with his children and servants. It goes on to the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow. Verse 14 repeats the same list for the feast of booths. Verse 12 gives the reason: “you were a slave in Egypt.” A feast kept only by the harvest’s owners is not the feast commanded here.
The king must live under the law

Verses 16–17 limit three things a king might gather: horses, wives, and treasure. Verse 16 ties horses to going back to Egypt, which is forbidden. Verses 18–19 give him a task: copy the law and read it daily. Verse 20 states the aim: “that his heart not be lifted up above his brothers.” The king is called a brother and stays under the same law as everyone. First Kings 10:26–11:4 reports that Solomon broke all three limits.
A prophet's claim requires attention to what actually happens

Verses 10–14 forbid the usual ways of learning the future: fortunes, omens, the dead. Verse 15 gives Israel a prophet in their place. That raises a problem, and verse 21 asks it openly. How can people tell a true word from a false one? Verse 22 gives a test anyone can apply: watch whether it happens. A failed word frees the people from fear of that speaker. Chapter 13 added a second test: a sign that comes true may still lead astray.
A serious accusation requires more than one person's assertion

A single accuser can be mistaken or can lie. Verse 15 says no charge of any kind stands on one voice. Two or three must agree. Verses 16–18 deal with a witness who lies on purpose. The judges must “make diligent inquisition” and not simply take his word. If he lied, he gets the penalty he sought for his brother (verse 19). So the court protects the accused as well as the victim.
The rules restrain some destruction while requiring other destruction

This chapter holds limits and harsh orders side by side. Verses 5–8 send men home for a house, a vineyard, a marriage, or fear. Verse 10 requires an offer of peace before a siege. Verses 16–17 order the complete destruction of the cities of the land. Verse 19 then protects fruit trees with a question: is the tree a man? An army will need that food later, and the tree has not fought anyone. The text restrains waste while it commands killing, and it does not reconcile the two.
A father's preference cannot remove every inheritance claim

Verse 15 pictures a man with two wives, one loved and one “hated.” Jacob’s house was like that, with Leah and Rachel (Genesis 29:30–31). The father might want to honor the loved wife’s son. Verse 16 says he may not. Verse 17 gives the double share to the actual firstborn, whoever his mother is. So a son’s right does not depend on his father’s feelings toward his mother. The law limits a father’s power inside his own house.
A home's design can create responsibility before anyone falls

Verse 8 assumes people will be up on the roof. It puts a duty on the builder before any accident happens. He must add a railing. If he does not and someone falls, the blood is “on your house.” So a person answers for a danger he could foresee and did not fix. Verses 1–4 say the same about a neighbor’s animals: “You may not hide yourself.” Doing nothing is treated as a choice.
An escaped servant receives protection from forced return

A runaway servant has no power, and his master has a claim on him. Verse 15 still forbids Israel to hand him over. Verse 16 goes further and gives him the choice of where to live. He may settle “where it pleases him best,” and no one may oppress him. Israel had itself fled from a master (Exodus 14:5). Verse 7 uses the same memory to forbid hating Egyptians. The rule places the escaped person’s safety above the owner’s claim.
Daily wages answer a need that cannot wait indefinitely

A day worker lives on that day’s pay. Verse 15 says he “is poor and sets his heart on it.” Holding the wage overnight keeps back what he needs now. The verse covers foreigners as well as Israelites (verse 14). It warns that the worker may cry to the LORD against the employer. Verses 6 and 10–13 protect the same people from lenders. Verse 18 gives the ground for all of it: “you were a slave in Egypt.”
Small measures can cause real harm

Goods were weighed against weights kept in a bag. Verse 13 pictures a cheat with two sets, one heavy and one light. The buyer has no way to test them. Verse 15 requires one “perfect and just” weight and measure. The reward promised is long life in the land, as for honoring parents (5:16). Verse 16 calls dishonest dealing an abomination to the LORD. An ancient trade weight shows the kind of tool the rule has in view.
Offering crops joins present abundance with a remembered vulnerable past

The giver stands at the altar with good fruit from his own land. His words in verse 5 start somewhere else: “a Syrian ready to perish.” He names an ancestor with no land and few people. Verses 6–8 go through slavery, a cry, and rescue. Only in verse 10 does he reach the basket. So the gift is set inside a history of weakness and help. Verse 11 then shares the joy with the Levite and the foreigner.
Public responses name wrongs that can remain hidden

Many of these twelve curses name acts done out of sight. Verse 15 says an idol set up “in secret,” and verse 24 a secret killing. A moved boundary stone or a bribe may never reach a court. Verse 18 names the blind traveler, who cannot see who misled him. So the list covers wrongs that witnesses and judges would miss. Each person says “Amen” aloud and binds himself. The public oath reaches where public law cannot.
The warnings describe the loss of an entire way of life

The blessings fill fourteen verses, and the curses fill fifty-four. Verse 47 gives the root of the curses in one line. Israel did not serve the LORD “with joyfulness” when it had “abundance of all things.” Verse 48 turns each good into its loss: hunger, thirst, nakedness, and lack. The chapter ends in Egypt, where the story of rescue began (verse 68). It warns a nation before it enters the land. It is not a rule for judging one sufferer.
The assembly includes people beyond its leaders and warriors

Verse 10 begins the list with heads, elders, and officers. Verse 11 goes on to little ones, wives, and foreigners in the camp. It ends with the lowest jobs: cutting wood and drawing water. All of them “stand today” before the LORD and enter the covenant. Verses 14–15 stretch it further, to people not yet born. So the covenant is not held only by leaders or fighting men. Verse 29 gives everyone the same task: do the words that have been revealed.
Near words still require a choice of action

Verses 12–13 answer two excuses before anyone makes them. The command is not up in heaven, and it is not across the sea. No one has to fetch it. Verse 14 says where it already is: “in your mouth and in your heart.” Moses has just spoken it, and they can repeat it. So the open question is not knowing but doing. Verse 19 names that step: “choose life.”
Public reading serves children who did not hear the first instruction

Moses is about to die, and the people who heard him will die too. Verse 9 puts the law in writing and in the priests’ care. Verses 10–11 set a fixed time to read it aloud: every seventh year. Verse 12 calls men, women, little ones, and foreigners to listen. Verse 13 adds the reason: children “who have not known” must hear it. Each new generation gets the words directly, not only by report. An Egyptian scribe’s palette shows the tools such writing needed.
The poem turns nourishment into an image of forgotten dependence

Verses 10–14 describe God feeding Israel: honey, oil, and the best of the field. Verse 15 shows what the feeding led to. The people “grew fat, and kicked,” like a well-fed animal that fights its owner. Then they left “the Rock” who saved them. Deuteronomy 8:12–14 warned of exactly this. The song gives Israel’s failure in advance, as a witness (31:19–21). Verse 36 still ends with compassion when their power is gone.
Tribal differences remain within a shared inheritance of instruction

Each tribe gets its own words, and the words differ widely. Levi has holy duties, Joseph rich land, Gad a lion’s strength. Verse 4 comes before all of them and names what they share. The law Moses gave is “an inheritance for the assembly of Jacob.” Land will be divided by tribe, but this inheritance is held in common. In Genesis 49:5–7 Jacob cursed Levi’s anger. Here Levi is trusted with the Urim and Thummim (verse 8).
The end preserves both succession and the loss of Moses

The book ends with a death and a handover in the same breath. Verse 8 gives the people thirty days to weep. Verse 9 says Joshua is ready, “for Moses had laid his hands on him.” The people listen to him, so the work goes on. Verse 10 does not let Joshua replace Moses in honor. No prophet since has been known by the LORD “face to face.” The loss is real, and the people still have a leader.
